doc.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Why oral history matters: history cannot be rewritten
summary: Baker and Jones agree that oral history prevents revisionism, since the people who lived each era preserve it, and that interviews should start earlier.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I thank God – I thank the good Lord that they cannot go back, like George Orwell’s 1986 or whatever the hell it was, and rewrite – and be revisionists about history. That’s why this oral history thing is so important.

Exactly. That’s one thing I think about all the time. I don’t give a damn what governmental control, no matter how sophisticated it gets – they can never go back and say, 1876 had this, 1951 had this, and 1964 had this, because it’s in the universe. You can’t even see it. It’s hanging there out in the clouds, and the people who were at that time, they will never lose – there’s millions and millions of people are holding it and preserving it in every era – the era of the string quartet, the era of the string bass, then the bass or whatever. That’s divinity.

I think that’s one of the governing reasons why it is so important to have the people who made these things happen, on record, because they used to wait until it was too late. Because they’re saying, if you start at 65, there are people who don’t make it to 45. Now the interviews are starting so much earlier, so that you don’t miss – if a Clifford Brown comes along, you don’t miss . . .
